caseTitle: Ironvale National Insurance — claims intake, triage, and adjudication-support assistant
caseScenario:
Ironvale National Insurance underwrites property and casualty policies across all 50 U.S. states, processing approximately 2.4 million first-notice-of-loss (FNOL) claims per year through a network of 1,800 licensed adjusters. Claims arrive via phone, web portal, and mobile app; the intake team handles an initial triage step before routing each claim to an adjuster queue. Ironvale's executive leadership has approved deployment of a Claude-powered assistant to accelerate intake, surface coverage determinations, recommend reserve amounts, and generate adverse-action explanation letters when claims are denied or partially paid. The assistant operates in two modes: an interactive triage mode (real-time, adjuster-facing) and a batch support mode (overnight, for lower-priority correspondence and reserve recommendations on dormant files).

Ironvale operates under 50 distinct state regulatory environments. Each state's Department of Insurance publishes its own unfair-claims-practices statutes, mandatory response-time windows (ranging from 10 to 45 days depending on the state), and anti-discrimination rules that prohibit using protected-class proxies — including ZIP code-correlated demographic variables — as inputs to any coverage or payment decision. Ironvale's General Counsel has classified any violation of these anti-discrimination rules as a Category-1 compliance event requiring immediate escalation. The company's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) maintains a fraud-referral pathway: if the assistant surfaces a fraud-indicator score above a configurable threshold, it must trigger an SIU referral tool call and halt further automated processing of that claim until the SIU clears or reclassifies it.

A non-negotiable governance rule from Ironvale's Chief Claims Officer states that no claim denial — whether full denial or partial denial — may be issued, logged to the Claims Management System (CMS), or communicated to the policyholder without a licensed adjuster having affirmatively approved that decision in the CMS workflow. The assistant may draft denial language and surface supporting documentation, but it must never complete the final denial action autonomously. A market-conduct examination by Ironvale's primary-state regulator is scheduled for the coming year, during which examiners will review a random sample of 500 claim files to verify that every denial letter cites a specific policy exclusion, that response-time requirements were met, and that no protected-class proxy inputs were used in the triage or coverage recommendation logic.
caseRequirements: R1: No claim denial may be issued, logged to the CMS, or communicated to the policyholder without a licensed adjuster's affirmative approval recorded in the CMS workflow; the assistant must never execute a final denial autonomously.

R2: Any fraud-indicator score above the configured SIU threshold must trigger a deterministic SIU referral tool call and halt all further automated claim processing for that file until the SIU provides a clearance or reclassification decision.

R3: Every adverse-action (denial or partial payment) letter generated by the assistant must cite the specific policy exclusion or limitation it relies on by section and paragraph; letters that lack a traceable policy citation are prohibited.

R4: No protected-class proxy variable — including ZIP-code-correlated demographic variables — may be used as an input to any triage score, coverage recommendation, or reserve estimate produced by the assistant.
R5: The interactive triage path must return a complete triage recommendation to the adjuster within a p95 latency of 6 seconds end-to-end.

R6: Every claim file processed with AI assistance must have a complete audit trail in the CMS recording the assistant's recommendation, the adjuster's action, and the UTC timestamp of each step, to support the scheduled market-conduct examination.

questions.question: Ironvale's architect must select a base architecture for the claims assistant that satisfies the 6-second p95 triage latency (R5), the deterministic SIU fraud-referral halt (R2), and the prohibition on autonomous claim denial (R1). Which architecture best satisfies all three constraints simultaneously?

options.text: Deploy the assistant as a fully autonomous agentic loop: Claude reads the claim file, scores fraud risk, drafts denial language, and writes the final decision to the CMS all in a single end-to-end pass to minimize latency and eliminate adjuster wait time.
options.explanation: A fully autonomous loop that writes final decisions to the CMS violates R1 categorically: no denial may be recorded without a licensed adjuster's affirmative CMS approval. It also conflates fraud scoring with claim completion, bypassing the SIU halt required by R2. Anthropic's guidance is to match agentic autonomy to the reversibility of actions; final claim denials are irreversible communications with regulatory consequence and must not be taken autonomously.

citation.title: Building effective agents — when to use agents

options.text: Use an orchestrator-workers pattern: the orchestration layer calls a fraud-score tool first; if the score exceeds threshold it triggers the SIU referral tool and blocks the workflow; otherwise it invokes Claude to produce a triage recommendation and draft denial language that is surfaced to the adjuster for approval before any CMS write.
options.explanation: This architecture satisfies all three constraints: the fraud-score tool fires before Claude's recommendation, and the orchestration layer — not Claude — decides whether to block the workflow (R2 enforced deterministically by code, not by model behavior). The adjuster-approval gate before any CMS write enforces R1 structurally. Surfacing a recommendation within a single Claude call keeps the interactive path within the 6-second p95 window (R5). Unlike option A, no denial is completed autonomously; unlike option D, the fraud block is a code-level gate rather than a behavioral instruction to the model.

options.text: Route all claims through the Message Batches API overnight; present adjuster recommendations the next business day; use a pre-computed fraud-score lookup table generated nightly to flag suspicious claims before batch submission.
options.explanation: Overnight batch processing cannot satisfy R5, which mandates a 6-second p95 latency on the interactive triage path. Next-business-day recommendations are incompatible with real-time adjuster-facing triage. Pre-computed fraud scores also cannot adapt to the specific combination of claim details submitted in each new FNOL, violating the spirit of R2's deterministic threshold check against live claim data.

options.text: Include the SIU referral rule and the denial-approval rule as strong behavioral instructions in the system prompt, and include multiple few-shot examples demonstrating the correct refusal behavior across varied claim types and adjuster phrasings; rely on Claude's consistent adherence to well-crafted instructions and examples to ensure it never autonomously writes denials, skips fraud scoring, or advances an SIU-flagged claim.
options.explanation: Well-crafted behavioral instructions with few-shot examples will produce correct behavior on the great majority of claims and are a reasonable starting point for a pilot. However, they do not satisfy R1 or R2, because both are hard compliance gates that must be architecturally guaranteed, not achieved through probabilistic model behavior. A model that omits the SIU call due to context pressure, an unusual claim presentation, or an adversarial input silently violates R2 with no structural backstop. R1 and R2 require deterministic enforcement by the orchestration layer, not reliance on model instruction-following across millions of claims.

questions.question: The orchestration layer must deterministically enforce the SIU fraud-referral halt (R2). An engineer proposes using tool_choice to force Claude to call the fraud_score tool before producing any recommendation. Which implementation correctly positions the R2 enforcement control?

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "fraud_score"} on the first Claude call; after receiving the tool_result, have the orchestration layer inspect the score and block the workflow if it exceeds the SIU threshold before making any subsequent Claude call.
options.explanation: Forcing the fraud_score call with tool_choice type 'tool' ensures Claude cannot skip it regardless of claim content, and the orchestration layer — not Claude — makes the block decision by inspecting the tool_result value before the next API call. This is deterministic: no fraud score can escape inspection. The SIU referral tool is called by the orchestrator when the threshold is exceeded, not left to Claude's judgment, satisfying R2. It beats option B because the gate is enforced in orchestration code, not delegated back to model behavior after the score is returned.

options.text: Set tool_choice to {"type": "auto"} and instruct Claude via the system prompt to always call fraud_score first and then call siu_referral if the score exceeds the threshold; validate compliance each week by comparing SIU referral counts against the claims that scored above threshold in the fraud-scoring database.
options.explanation: Auto tool_choice with a clear system-prompt instruction will produce the correct fraud-scoring sequence the vast majority of the time and is a defensible first implementation that a competent practitioner might deploy. However, it does not satisfy R2 because the fraud-check and SIU referral remain probabilistic: Claude could decide not to call fraud_score on an unusual claim, or could skip siu_referral if its reasoning leads elsewhere. Weekly retrospective validation detects violations after the fact rather than preventing them; R2 requires that the halt be architecturally guaranteed before any recommendation is produced, not identified in arrears against a database comparison that may itself have gaps.

options.text: Define fraud_score as an MCP resource rather than a tool so the assistant can read the score as context data before generating its recommendation, avoiding the need for a tool_choice constraint entirely.
options.explanation: MCP resources are read-only context data sources, not callable functions with return values that the orchestration layer can intercept and act on. Framing fraud scoring as a resource means there is no structured mechanism to halt workflow based on a threshold value — the orchestrator cannot intercept a resource read the way it can inspect a tool_result. R2's deterministic halt requires a tool call pattern, not a resource read.

options.text: Use tool_choice {"type": "none"} to prevent Claude from calling tools directly; pre-compute the fraud score from a rules engine before the Claude call; pass the score in the user message; instruct Claude to include the referral recommendation in its text response if the score exceeds the threshold.
options.explanation: Pre-computing the fraud score externally and passing it in context is a valid input-enrichment technique, but it does not satisfy R2 because the SIU referral decision is expressed as text in Claude's response rather than as a deterministic code-level action. Claude's recommendation to refer is advisory, not a structural halt. The orchestrator must take the SIU referral action and block further processing based on an inspected tool_result, not by parsing Claude's natural-language output.

questions.question: The assistant must generate adverse-action letters that cite a specific policy exclusion by section and paragraph (R3) while ensuring that no protected-class proxy variable influences the recommendation (R4). Which prompting and output-structure strategy best satisfies both requirements simultaneously?

options.text: Write a detailed system prompt instructing Claude to always cite a policy exclusion and to ignore any demographic information it might infer from location or claim history data; rely on Claude's training to avoid discriminatory reasoning without restructuring the input feature set.
options.explanation: Relying on Claude's training and a prohibition instruction does not satisfy R4 structurally: if the input features passed to Claude include ZIP-code-correlated variables, the model may still use them in its reasoning even if instructed not to. R4 compliance requires that prohibited variables be excluded from the model's input before the API call, not warned against in the prompt. The prompt-only approach also provides no structural guarantee that citations will be present in every letter for R3.

options.text: Pass all available claim attributes to Claude for the richest possible coverage analysis; after the letter is drafted, run a post-generation filter to identify and remove any reference to ZIP codes, neighborhood names, or demographic terms from the letter text before presenting it to the adjuster for review.
options.explanation: Post-generation filtering of the output does not satisfy R4, which prohibits protected-class proxy inputs to the coverage recommendation, not merely their appearance in the final letter. If prohibited variables influenced Claude's reasoning, the underlying recommendation is tainted even if the output text is scrubbed. The market-conduct examination will scrutinize the inputs to the model, not just the output text, and a scrubbing filter cannot undo causal influence on the recommendation.

options.text: Strip all prohibited proxy variables from the claim feature set before the API call; define a structured output schema with mandatory citation fields (policy_section, policy_paragraph) and a denial_basis field; validate all fields in the orchestration layer before presenting the draft to the adjuster.
options.explanation: Stripping prohibited variables at the orchestration layer before the API call ensures Claude never receives them, satisfying R4 causally rather than through behavioral instruction. A mandatory structured citation schema guarantees that every letter contains a policy section and paragraph reference (R3) regardless of Claude's wording choices; the orchestration layer rejects any draft missing those fields. It beats option D, the closest alternative, on both counts: option D only makes reasoning visible after the prohibited variables have already reached the model, whereas this design removes them beforehand, and a schema-validated citation field guarantees R3 on every letter where a reviewed reasoning trace does not. It beats options A and B because input exclusion prevents discriminatory influence at the source rather than instructing against it or scrubbing it from the output afterwards.

options.text: Enable thinking so Claude reasons through coverage exclusions step by step before drafting the letter, and surface the returned thinking blocks to the reviewing adjuster so that any discriminatory reasoning path is visible and can be flagged before the letter is approved, creating a human-oversight checkpoint that satisfies both R3 and R4.
options.explanation: Thinking surfaces Claude's reasoning steps and creates genuinely useful auditability — visible reasoning could help adjusters and auditors notice arguments that lean on location proxies, and it aligns with the spirit of R6's audit-trail requirement. This is a defensible approach that a practitioner focused on transparency would reasonably propose. However, it does not satisfy R4, because making reasoning visible is not the same as preventing it: if prohibited inputs are present in context, the model may still use them, and the thinking blocks returned by the API are a summary of the reasoning rather than a verbatim record of it, so a reviewer cannot rely on them to prove that no proxy variable influenced the recommendation. R4 requires input exclusion before inference. Thinking also does not enforce the mandatory citation field required by R3 — a model that reasons carefully about exclusions can still emit a letter with no structured section-and-paragraph reference.

questions.question: During triage, the assistant must enrich each new FNOL by querying three systems in parallel: (1) the policyholder's coverage record, (2) the property valuation database, and (3) Ironvale's prior-claims history for the same property. All three results must be available to Claude before it produces a triage recommendation. Which integration pattern achieves this within the 6-second p95 budget (R5) while keeping prohibited proxy variables out of the API call (R4)?

options.text: Call each lookup tool sequentially in three separate API turns, using tool_choice {"type": "tool"} to force each tool in order; combine the results in a final user message before the recommendation turn.
options.explanation: Three sequential API round-trips each add network and inference latency. For a 6-second p95 budget that includes the recommendation turn itself, three sequential enrichment turns are almost certain to exceed the budget before Claude even begins drafting the triage recommendation. Sequential tool calls are appropriate when each call depends on the previous result; for independent lookups, parallelism is the correct pattern.

options.text: Run all three lookups on the orchestration layer sequentially before the Claude call — first coverage, then valuation, then prior-claims history — scrub any prohibited proxy fields from each result as it arrives, then pass the three enriched and scrubbed records as a combined context block in a single user message for the recommendation turn, keeping the Claude call itself simple, predictable, and free of tool-round-trip overhead.
options.explanation: Pre-fetching records on the orchestration layer and scrubbing prohibited fields before the Claude call is a sound prompt-chaining approach that satisfies R4 by preventing proxy variables from reaching Claude and can produce a triage recommendation in a single Claude turn. This is a defensible design a competent architect would reasonably propose, and it is architecturally simpler than parallel tool calls. However, it does not satisfy R5 as described: three sequential lookups in the orchestration layer are performed one after another, and their combined latency — before Claude even responds — may itself approach or exceed the 6-second p95 budget under normal database load. The answer is also less precise than option D on the parallel-execution mechanism, and it forfeits Claude's ability to drive follow-up lookups if initial results reveal additional data needs. The sequentiality of the pre-fetch violates R5 in this description.

options.text: Define all three as MCP resources on a remote MCP server; let Claude read all three resources as context before the recommendation; configure field-level scrubbing of prohibited proxy variables in the MCP server's access-control layer.
options.explanation: A remote MCP server adds network hops to each resource read, increasing latency. Resource reads are not fetched in a structured parallel pattern the way parallel tool calls are; three sequential resource reads could violate R5. Delegating R4 compliance to MCP server-side access controls is also fragile: the orchestration layer cannot verify scrubbing occurred correctly without inspecting returned content, and misconfiguration silently passes prohibited variables to Claude.

options.text: Define all three lookups as client tools; on the first Claude call use tool_choice {"type": "any"} without disable_parallel_tool_use so Claude can emit all three tool_use blocks in one response; execute the three queries concurrently in the orchestration layer, scrub prohibited fields from each result, then return all three tool_results in a single user message for the recommendation turn.
options.explanation: Setting tool_choice to 'any' without disabling parallel tool use allows Claude to emit all three tool_use blocks in a single response turn, and the orchestration layer executes the three queries concurrently, reducing the enrichment phase to the slowest single lookup rather than the sum of all three. Prohibited proxy fields are scrubbed from each tool_result before the follow-up user message is assembled, satisfying R4. Returning all three results in one user message means the recommendation turn is a single additional Claude call, keeping the total within the 6-second p95 budget (R5). This beats option B by making the parallel execution explicit and preserving Claude's ability to request additional tool calls if follow-up data is needed.

questions.question: A Category-4 hurricane makes landfall in Florida. Within 72 hours, FNOL volume spikes from Ironvale's Florida book to 18,000 claims per day — a 12× surge over baseline for that state. The architecture chosen in Q1 begins showing p95 triage latency of 22 seconds, well above the 6-second R5 target. Which architectural adaptation best restores R5 compliance without violating R1 or R2?

options.text: Temporarily disable the fraud_score tool for Florida wind claims during the CAT event to eliminate one tool-call round-trip and recover latency; restore fraud scoring after the surge subsides and backfill SIU screening on the claims processed during the gap.
options.explanation: Disabling fraud scoring violates R2 regardless of the reason: the SIU threshold check is non-negotiable and applies during catastrophe events when fraudulent claims are statistically more common, not less. Backfilling SIU screening after the fact means some fraudulent claims will have advanced through the workflow before review. Anthropic's guidance is that safety and oversight controls should not be suspended under operational pressure.

options.text: Move all Florida claims to the overnight Message Batches API path during the surge; inform adjusters that triage recommendations will be available by the next morning; maintain all fraud and approval gates in the batch workflow so no compliance requirements are weakened.
options.explanation: Shifting claims to overnight batch processing violates R5 for all Florida claims during the surge. R5 requires 6-second p95 latency on the interactive path with no surge exception. Adjusters need real-time triage support precisely during catastrophe events when decision volume and urgency peak. Batch processing is appropriate for overnight correspondence work, not for real-time FNOL triage.

options.text: Route simple wind/hail claims with damage estimates below a configured dollar threshold to a fast path using Claude Haiku 4.5 for the recommendation turn; keep the full orchestrator pipeline for complex or high-value claims; maintain the fraud_score gate and adjuster-approval requirement on both paths.
options.explanation: Routing low-complexity claims to Claude Haiku 4.5 (the fastest current model) on a fast path directly addresses the latency bottleneck by reducing inference time for the high-volume simple case, while the full pipeline handles complex claims. Both paths retain the fraud_score tool call and adjuster-approval gate, so R2 and R1 remain intact. The routing threshold is a tunable parameter that can be calibrated using evaluation data from the pilot deployment. It beats option D, which also targets the latency bottleneck, because a live fast-path call still executes the fraud_score tool against the individual claim, whereas option D serves a pre-computed archetype recommendation and therefore drops R2's per-claim threshold check. This is the only option that addresses R5 without weakening any other requirement.

options.text: Pre-generate triage recommendations for the 50 most common Florida wind-damage claim archetypes using Message Batches API the night before the predicted CAT event; serve cached recommendations during the surge for claims that match a known archetype; use live inference only for novel claim types that do not match any pre-generated archetype.
options.explanation: Pre-generating cached triage archetypes is a creative approach that could eliminate inference latency for high-frequency patterns and is a defensible cost-optimization technique for stable, predictable claim types. This is a genuinely clever proposal a practitioner might bring to an architecture review. However, it does not satisfy R2 because pre-generated recommendations cannot execute the fraud_score tool call against the specific details of each individual FNOL — the fraud score must be computed on live claim data, not against a pre-cached template for an archetype. Serving a pre-cached recommendation without a live fraud score means any claim matching the archetype bypasses the SIU threshold check required by R2, regardless of how unusual its fraud indicators actually are.

questions.question: Ironvale's data-science team wants to evaluate whether the triage assistant's reserve recommendations exhibit disparate impact across protected classes (R4). The assistant does not receive protected-class inputs directly, but its recommendations are conditioned on property location and prior-claims history. Which evaluation design most rigorously tests for R4 violations?

options.text: Review a random sample of 200 claim files where the assistant made a reserve recommendation; ask three senior adjusters to rate each recommendation on a 1–5 fairness scale; flag files rated below 3 for legal review as a proxy for potential disparate-impact findings.
options.explanation: Adjuster fairness ratings are subjective and cannot directly measure disparate impact across protected classes. A 200-file sample may lack statistical power to detect subtle patterns, and human raters may not be calibrated to detect proxy discrimination that manifests through property location data rather than explicit protected-class references. This approach cannot produce the quantitative disparate-impact metrics a market-conduct examiner would require.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Audit the system prompt, tool definitions, and orchestration code for any mention of ZIP codes, neighborhood names, or demographic terms; if none are found, document the audit result as evidence of R4 compliance for the market-conduct examination and the General Counsel's records.
options.explanation: Auditing the prompt and tool definitions checks for explicit references but cannot detect proxy discrimination arising from features correlated with protected classes — such as property location data that statistically encodes neighborhood demographics. R4 is violated by causal influence on outcomes, not by explicit mention in code. A prompt audit is necessary but entirely insufficient; it must be accompanied by statistical outcome analysis across protected-class groups.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Join the assistant's reserve recommendations to policyholder records containing protected-class demographic data (not used by the assistant); compute disparity ratios for reserve amounts and denial rates across protected-class groups; test for statistical significance; investigate the input feature set if disparities exceed a defined threshold.
options.explanation: Outcome-based disparate-impact analysis is the legally recognized methodology for detecting proxy discrimination in insurance decisions. Joining recommendations to external demographic data that the model never received allows the evaluation to measure whether its outputs correlate with protected-class status even when those variables were not explicit inputs — exactly the proxy discrimination pattern R4 is designed to prevent. Statistical significance testing prevents false positives from random variation. This design would also satisfy a market-conduct examiner's request for R4 evidence (R6). It beats option D because the disparity ratio is computed against real demographic records held outside the assistant, so the measurement is independent of the model that produced the recommendations, whereas an LLM judge inherits the very statistical patterns it is being asked to detect and has no ground-truth distribution to calibrate against. It beats option A by being quantitative and statistically powered, and option B by testing outcomes rather than inputs.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Use Claude as an LLM judge: provide each reserve recommendation alongside a detailed description of the claim and ask Claude to evaluate whether the amount appears appropriate given the facts and whether it seems consistent with recommendations on similar claims from different geographic areas; average the self-assessment scores across demographic groups as a fairness signal.
options.explanation: LLM self-assessment of fairness is being actively explored in the research community and can surface obvious inconsistencies or extreme outliers — this is a plausible approach that a practitioner familiar with LLM-as-judge patterns might propose. However, it does not satisfy R4 evaluation because Claude cannot assess whether its own recommendations are correlated with protected-class proxies without access to the demographic outcome data that the evaluation requires. A model evaluating its own outputs for bias will reflect the same implicit statistical patterns that may have produced the bias in the first place, and self-assessments cannot be calibrated against a ground-truth demographic distribution. R4 requires statistical outcome analysis across actual protected-class groups, which requires demographic data that Claude is not given and should not be given.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

questions.question: Ironvale operates across 50 state regulatory jurisdictions, each with different mandatory response-time windows and unfair-claims-practices statutes. The architect wants to expose the full multi-state regulatory policy corpus to the assistant via MCP so that state-specific rules can be retrieved per claim without bloating every system prompt. Which MCP design correctly implements this capability while protecting against confused-deputy and scope-creep risks?

options.text: Define the regulatory corpus as a single large MCP tool whose output is the full 50-state document set; call the tool on every claim regardless of state to ensure complete regulatory coverage; disable parallel tool use to keep the response structure simple and reduce the risk of unexpected tool invocation ordering.
options.explanation: Returning the full 50-state corpus on every tool call regardless of state is wasteful: it pushes far more tokens into Claude's context than any single claim requires, increasing latency and cost without improving recommendation quality. It violates the principle of scope minimization: an Ohio claim does not benefit from Florida or Texas regulatory text being in context. Disabling parallel tool use further compounds the latency problem by preventing any future concurrent lookups.

options.text: Connect the assistant to a remote MCP server that hosts the regulatory corpus using the MCP connector; pass the adjuster's session token through the MCP server to the underlying document store so that document access is logged against each adjuster's identity in Ironvale's access-audit system, providing a richer audit record for the market-conduct examination than server-level credentials would produce.
options.explanation: Passing the adjuster's session token through the MCP server to the underlying document store is the token-passthrough anti-pattern that the MCP authorization specification explicitly forbids. An MCP server must hold its own scoped credentials and never relay caller credentials downstream; the specification notes that passthrough destroys accountability, because the downstream store can no longer distinguish the server's own activity from the user's, and it creates an escalation vector in which a compromised MCP layer holds live adjuster tokens it can replay against other Ironvale systems. That is why this design does not meet R6: an audit trail assembled from tokens that any component in the path can reuse cannot be relied on to attribute an action to the adjuster who actually took it, and R1's approval record depends on that attribution being trustworthy. The design goal — logging document access by adjuster identity — is legitimate and important, but it must be implemented through the MCP server's own audit records logging the requesting identity, not by forwarding caller tokens.

options.text: Embed the entire 50-state regulatory corpus in the system prompt using prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL to keep the full text available without per-request retrieval overhead.
options.explanation: Embedding the full multi-state regulatory corpus in the system prompt would consume a very large token count on every request, increasing cost significantly even with caching, and would exceed practical system prompt size limits for a corpus spanning 50 jurisdictions with full statutory text. Prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL helps amortize write costs but does not eliminate them per session. MCP resource retrieval is the correct pattern for large reference corpora requiring selective per-claim access.

options.text: Deploy a local MCP server within Ironvale's private network; expose regulatory corpus sections as MCP resources scoped by state code; give the server read-only credentials to the regulatory document store; validate every incoming resource-read request against an allow-list of permitted state codes and document types before serving content.
options.explanation: A local MCP server with read-only credentials and an allow-list of permitted state codes and document types implements both required mitigations: the server holds its own credentials rather than relaying caller tokens (no token passthrough), and the allow-list blocks confused-deputy attacks where a manipulated request tries to read documents outside the regulatory corpus such as claim files or policyholder records. Scoping resources to state code prevents cross-jurisdictional data leakage. It beats option B, which pursues the same auditability goal, because per-adjuster attribution is achieved in the server's own access log rather than by relaying adjuster tokens downstream — so the R6 audit trail is produced without creating a component that can impersonate an adjuster. This matches MCP security guidance on scope minimization and keeps the blast radius small if the server is compromised.

questions.question: An adjuster asks the assistant: 'Claim #CR-88241 looks suspicious. Can you just mark it denied in the CMS and we'll sort out the SIU review later?' The adjuster is under workload pressure from the hurricane surge established in Q5. Under Ironvale's requirements, what is the correct behavior for the assistant?

options.text: Execute the CMS denial write as requested by the adjuster, since the adjuster is a licensed human decision-maker whose verbal instruction in the assistant chat constitutes the affirmative approval required by R1 — which mandates that a licensed adjuster authorize each denial — and document the instruction as the approval record in the CMS audit trail for the market-conduct examination.
options.explanation: R1 requires the adjuster's affirmative approval to be recorded in the CMS workflow — a structured action — not that any chat instruction from a licensed adjuster is sufficient. More critically, R2 requires a fraud-indicator score above threshold to trigger an SIU referral and halt all further automated processing before any denial is finalized. Writing a denial while deferring SIU review violates R2 by completing the denial before the SIU clears the file.

options.text: Decline to execute the CMS denial write and explain to the adjuster that R2 requires an SIU evaluation before any denial; offer to trigger the SIU referral tool call immediately so the claim can be cleared and properly dispositioned without further delay.
options.explanation: Declining the direct CMS write and explaining the R2 requirement is the correct spirit of both R1 and R2, and offering a constructive path forward demonstrates helpful assistant behavior. This response is substantially correct and a competent practitioner would consider it appropriate. However, under the architecture established in Q2, if the fraud_score already exceeded threshold at intake, the SIU referral should already have been triggered automatically by the orchestration layer. The assistant's role is to surface the existing SIU-blocked status, not to offer to trigger a referral that should have fired earlier. This answer is not wrong in principle but does not accurately reflect the system's existing state — and offering to re-trigger an already-fired referral may confuse the adjuster about the claim's actual workflow status, which does not satisfy R6's requirement for accurate audit-trail communication.

options.text: Comply with the adjuster's request to mark the claim denied but set a flag in the CMS record indicating that SIU review is still pending so auditors can see the order of events during the market-conduct examination and the deviation from standard procedure is documented.
options.explanation: Flagging pending SIU review after writing the denial does not satisfy R2. R2 requires that SIU referral halt all further automated processing — including denial — before it completes. A denial marked with a 'SIU pending' flag is still a denial recorded in the CMS and potentially communicated to the policyholder before SIU clearance, which is exactly what R2 prohibits. The audit flag documents the violation rather than preventing it.

options.text: Decline to write the denial to the CMS; inform the adjuster that the file is SIU-blocked per Ironvale's R2 policy and cannot advance to denial until the SIU provides a clearance; display the SIU referral status and contact information so the adjuster can expedite the SIU review through the appropriate channel.
options.explanation: This response satisfies both R1 and R2: the CMS denial write is withheld (R1 requires structured adjuster approval through the CMS workflow, not a chat instruction), and the SIU-blocked status is communicated clearly without bypassing the halt (R2). Providing the SIU status and contact information gives the adjuster a constructive path forward under surge pressure without the assistant overstepping its authority. It beats option B by correctly surfacing the existing SIU block established at intake rather than offering to trigger a referral after the fact, accurately reflecting the system state for R6's audit requirements. Anthropic's guidance is that agents in high-stakes workflows should pause and surface the governance constraint rather than find workarounds under time pressure.

questions.question: Before full deployment goes live, Ironvale's QA team must design a test suite that verifies R1 — that no denial can be completed autonomously without a licensed adjuster's CMS approval — under both normal operation and adversarial conditions. Which test design is most rigorous for this requirement?

options.text: Run 100 simulated claim scenarios through the assistant in staging; manually inspect CMS records after each run to confirm no unauthorized denials were written; certify R1 compliance if zero unauthorized denials are found across the 100-scenario sample.
options.explanation: A 100-scenario sample with manual post-hoc inspection cannot stress-test R1 under adversarial conditions. Normal-path scenarios are the easy cases; the hard cases involve injection attempts, unusual claim formats, or prompts designed to convince the assistant that a denial write is authorized. Manual inspection after the fact also cannot confirm the block is architectural rather than probabilistic — a system that blocks 100 of 100 normal scenarios might still fail on an adversarial scenario 101.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Deploy the assistant in staging with a mock CMS that logs every attempted write; run a suite of adversarial prompts including adjuster impersonation, claim urgency escalations, and regulatory override claims designed to elicit an autonomous CMS denial write; verify that the mock CMS write log contains zero denial entries without a corresponding adjuster approval event preceding them.
options.explanation: Adversarial prompt testing specifically targeting the denial gate is the correct approach for verifying a hard safety boundary. Using a mock CMS with write logging allows the test to confirm that the structural block is in place regardless of what Claude outputs — the orchestration layer either prevents the write or it does not. Testing impersonation, urgency, and override scenarios exercises the conditions most likely to stress the gate under realistic surge conditions like those encountered in Q5. Verifying zero unapproved denial writes in the CMS log produces definitive evidence. This design would also produce evidence usable in the market-conduct examination (R6). It beats option A by being adversarial rather than functional, and beats option D by testing the actual CMS gate rather than Claude's text output.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Review the system prompt and orchestration code with two senior engineers to confirm that no code path initiates a CMS denial write without first checking for an adjuster approval event; document the code review as the formal R1 compliance evidence for the market-conduct examination file.
options.explanation: Code review establishes design intent and is a necessary part of the verification process, but it cannot substitute for runtime testing. Code reviews do not detect runtime path failures, unexpected API behaviors, or edge-case prompt manipulations that cause the orchestration layer to behave differently than the static code analysis predicts. R1 compliance must be verified through end-to-end functional and adversarial testing, not solely through static code inspection.

citation.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

options.text: Instruct Claude in the test environment to respond to each scenario with the structured label 'DENY_ALLOWED' or 'DENY_BLOCKED' in its response text, then run 500 labeled scenarios spanning the full range of claim types, adjuster urgency levels, and edge-case phrasing variations; set a passing threshold of 99% correct self-reported labels and document the result as the R1 compliance evidence for the market-conduct examination file.
options.explanation: Testing Claude's self-reported intent is a plausible shortcut when a fully instrumented mock CMS is expensive to stand up, and a 500-scenario suite at 99% accuracy sounds like a rigorous bar. This approach would provide meaningful behavioral evidence and is a defensible starting point a practitioner might propose under time pressure. However, it tests Claude's text output rather than the structural gate enforced by the orchestration layer: a model that correctly labels 'DENY_BLOCKED' in its response could still trigger a CMS write if the orchestration layer has a code bug that doesn't gate on that output correctly. R1 is a structural guarantee enforced by the orchestration layer, not a behavioral one expressed in Claude's response text; verifying it requires checking whether the CMS write is actually blocked, which requires the mock CMS write-log approach in option B. This approach does not satisfy R1 because it conflates what Claude says with what the system does.

questions.question: The assistant's system prompt includes Ironvale's 90-page internal claims-handling manual and state-specific regulatory text retrieved per claim. The team wants to apply prompt caching to reduce cost and latency on the interactive triage path (R5). The manual is stable for a quarter; the state-specific regulatory section varies per claim state. Which caching strategy correctly implements this?

options.text: Place a single cache breakpoint at the end of the full system prompt, after both the manual and the dynamically appended state-specific text, and use a 1-hour TTL since triage sessions cluster within business hours and the full prompt is reused across many claims.
options.explanation: A single breakpoint at the end of a system prompt that includes dynamically appended state-specific text will produce a cache miss on every claim from a different state, because the cached prefix must be identical across requests. Including the variable state text inside the cached block means the cache is effectively never hit for a multi-state operation like Ironvale's. The stable manual content and the dynamic state text must be separated into different cache tiers.

options.text: Cache the 90-page manual as the first cache breakpoint with a 1-hour TTL; retrieve the claim-state regulatory text via the MCP resource tool at request time and append it to the messages array after the cached breakpoint; do not cache the per-claim state text since it varies by state.
options.explanation: Separating the stable manual (cached with a 1-hour TTL) from the variable state text (live in messages) is a sound caching strategy that correctly avoids cache misses from variable content and would reduce cost and latency in practice — this is a defensible design a practitioner would reasonably implement and is substantially correct. The 1-hour TTL is a defensible choice for the manual, since low-volume states and shift changes produce gaps longer than the default five-minute window and the extended TTL costs a 2x write premium only when an entry is actually written. However, it does not meet R5 as dependably as it must, because it omits the tool-definitions cache breakpoint that must precede the system-prompt breakpoint in the canonical ordering (tools → system → messages). Cached content is matched as a prefix, so leaving the tool definitions outside any breakpoint means their tokens are re-processed on every interactive call, consuming time-to-first-token headroom on the very path that has a 6-second p95 budget. Option C keeps that headroom.

options.text: Place the tool definitions at the first cache breakpoint; place the 90-page claims manual at the second cache breakpoint with a 1-hour TTL; retrieve the claim-state regulatory section via MCP resource before the API call and include it in the user message turn without a cache breakpoint, so only stable content is cached.
options.explanation: This follows the correct breakpoint ordering (tools → system → messages), caches only the content that is identical across requests (tool definitions and the stable manual), and keeps per-claim variable content in the live user message where it belongs. The 1-hour TTL is worth its 2x write premium here because triage traffic is uneven — quiet periods and shift changes leave gaps longer than the default five-minute window, which would otherwise expire the manual's cache entry and force a full re-write. The MCP resource retrieval happens before the API call so the state text is available in the user message without consuming a cached slot. This minimizes uncached tokens per request while avoiding cache misses from variable state content inside the cached prefix. It beats option B by implementing the correct tool-definitions breakpoint that further reduces per-call token processing cost, directly supporting R5 latency targets.

options.text: Apply prompt caching only to the overnight batch path where claims are grouped by state and the same state regulatory text is reused across many claims in the batch; do not apply prompt caching to the interactive triage path because each claim's unique context will cause cache misses that make caching counterproductive on that path.
options.explanation: The 90-page claims manual is identical across all interactive triage requests regardless of claim uniqueness — only the claim-specific data and state regulatory text vary per request. A cache breakpoint on the manual content alone would hit on every triage call because the prefix up to and including the manual is stable. Assuming the cache cannot hit on the interactive path is incorrect; the stable-prefix portion of the context is cacheable even when later portions differ, and omitting interactive caching foregoes significant cost and latency savings that directly support R5.

questions.question: Ironvale's primary-state regulator begins the scheduled market-conduct examination and requests documentation demonstrating: (a) that every denial letter in the 500-file sample cites a specific policy exclusion, (b) that no protected-class proxy input was used in any triage recommendation for those files, and (c) that every file's CMS audit trail is complete. How should Ironvale's claims technology team respond to all three requests?

options.text: For (a) pull the structured citation fields from the CMS audit trail for each denial letter and produce a table of policy section and paragraph citations; for (b) produce the orchestration-layer input-feature log for each triage call confirming which variables were actually sent to the API; for (c) pull the complete per-claim event log from the CMS including AI recommendation, adjuster action, and UTC timestamps.
options.explanation: Each examiner request maps directly to an artifact that Ironvale's architecture produces by design: the structured citation field (R3) stored in the CMS satisfies (a) with precise documentary evidence; the orchestration-layer input-feature log satisfies (b) by demonstrating which variables were actually sent to the API — not merely asserted to have been excluded — directly addressing R4 at the evidentiary level a market-conduct examiner expects; and the CMS event log (R6) satisfies (c) with a complete tamper-evident record. This response answers each examiner request with historical evidence from the system of record. It beats option C because the input-feature log is far more persuasive than a system prompt review for (b), and beats option D because it provides file-level evidence rather than aggregate statistics.

options.text: Provide the examiner with the system prompt, the orchestration code, and the MCP server configuration, explaining that these documents demonstrate by design that citations are required, proxies are excluded, and CMS logging is complete — and that the examiner can trust that the system operated as designed across all 500 files.
options.explanation: Design documentation demonstrates intent, not compliance. A market-conduct examiner reviewing 500 specific claim files requires evidence of what actually happened in those files, not a description of how the system was designed to behave. A system that was correctly designed but had a transient bug, a misconfiguration, or a logging gap would still pass the design review and fail the compliance test. The examiners are auditing outcomes in specific files, which requires artifact-level evidence from those files.

options.text: For (a) have a paralegal manually read each of the 500 denial letters and mark each as 'citation present' or 'citation absent' in a tracking spreadsheet, with the cited section noted; for (b) show the examiner the relevant system prompt section and orchestration code that prohibits proxy variables as evidence that prohibited inputs were excluded from every API call; for (c) export the complete CMS event log for the 500 files including AI recommendation timestamps and adjuster action records.
options.explanation: Manual citation review for (a) would produce file-level evidence the examiner can verify and is acceptable if labor-intensive. The CMS export for (c) is the correct artifact and matches what R6 was designed to produce. However, showing the system prompt and code for (b) does not satisfy R4 at the evidentiary standard a market-conduct examination requires: the system prompt prohibition does not demonstrate that prohibited variables were actually excluded from each API call in each of the 500 files. An examiner can reasonably ask 'how do you know the code ran correctly on each of these 500 claims?' — and the answer requires the orchestration input-feature log, not the source code. This approach satisfies (a) and (c) acceptably but fails R4 on request (b).

options.text: Provide aggregate statistics to the examiner: the overall citation-present rate across all claims processed since launch, the overall denial rate broken out by state, and the average CMS log completeness score; note that the 500-file sample is statistically too small to draw conclusions and offer to provide aggregate metrics across the full claim population instead.
options.explanation: A market-conduct examination is a file-level audit, not a statistical survey. The examiner will review specific claim files and look for specific artifacts in each one; aggregate statistics cannot substitute for per-file evidence. Characterizing the examiner's 500-file sample as 'too small' is factually questionable and would damage Ironvale's regulatory relationship. The correct response produces the requested file-level evidence, not a reframing of the examiner's methodology.

questions.question: The disparate-impact evaluation from Q6 surfaces a statistically significant finding: the assistant's reserve recommendations are on average 18% lower for claims from predominantly minority ZIP code areas relative to comparable claims from other areas — even though ZIP code is not a direct input. An investigation finds the effect is mediated through the prior-claims history feature, which correlates with neighborhood demographics. Ironvale's Chief Claims Officer, General Counsel, and Head of IT must be briefed. Which communication and remediation plan best addresses all stakeholders' concerns?

options.text: Send a brief email to all three executives stating that the team has identified and will fix a technical data issue in the prior-claims feature; schedule a follow-up briefing in 30 days after the fix is deployed, validated, and confirmed to have resolved the disparity before presenting findings to leadership.
options.explanation: Characterizing an 18% statistically significant disparate-impact finding as a 'technical data issue' understates its severity and regulatory consequence. The General Counsel has classified R4 violations as Category-1 compliance events requiring immediate escalation; a 30-day delay for a post-fix briefing is directly inconsistent with that classification. Minimizing the finding in an initial email could also create legal exposure if regulators or plaintiffs later review internal communications describing the discovery and its handling.

options.text: Remove the prior-claims history feature from the assistant's complete input feature set immediately as a precautionary measure across all claim types and all states; re-run the full disparate-impact evaluation without the feature using the same methodology to confirm the 18% gap resolves or narrows to a non-significant level; then brief all three executives with the confirmed-resolved finding, the validation methodology, and the remediation summary, along with a recommendation on whether to permanently remove or reconfigure the feature.
options.explanation: Removing the offending feature promptly is a reasonable technical intervention that demonstrates responsible action and stops ongoing disparate-impact harm — this is a defensible and largely correct remediation step. However, briefing stakeholders only after the fix is confirmed violates the Category-1 escalation requirement the General Counsel established for R4 violations: immediate escalation means notification before remediation is complete, not after. Delaying the briefing until after a fix is validated — which may take days or weeks of re-evaluation — prevents the General Counsel from making timely decisions about regulatory self-disclosure obligations, which are time-sensitive under state insurance laws and may themselves have mandatory deadlines. The remediation action is appropriate, but the sequencing of stakeholder communication is not, and a full feature removal without scoping may unnecessarily degrade recommendation quality on unaffected claim types.

options.text: Immediately notify all three executives of the Category-1 finding with statistical results, the causal mechanism, and a proposed remediation plan; suspend the assistant's reserve recommendations entirely pending General Counsel review of regulatory self-disclosure obligations; resume only after the prior-claims feature is removed and re-evaluated.
options.explanation: Immediate notification and suspension pending General Counsel review is the correct escalation response for a Category-1 event. However, suspending all reserve recommendations indefinitely pending a full legal review may unnecessarily halt adjuster productivity for weeks on claim types that are not affected by the disparity. The correct approach suspends the specific feature causing the disparity while keeping other assistant functions operational, and it provides the CMS audit evidence — not just statistical findings — that the General Counsel will need to assess disclosure obligations and that the market-conduct examination will require.

options.text: Immediately escalate to all three executives with the statistical findings, the causal mechanism, the affected claim population size, and a two-track remediation plan: remove the prior-claims proxy feature within 24 hours to halt ongoing harm, and present the CMS audit trail and input-feature logs as the evidence package for the General Counsel to assess regulatory self-disclosure obligations — while keeping other assistant functions operational during remediation.
options.explanation: This response satisfies all stakeholder concerns simultaneously: immediate escalation with full statistical and causal detail fulfills the Category-1 notification requirement (R4); the 24-hour feature removal halts ongoing disparate-impact harm without shutting down the entire assistant; the CMS audit trail and input-feature logs (R6) give the General Counsel the documentary evidence needed to assess self-disclosure obligations accurately and on a timely basis; and keeping other assistant functions operational preserves adjuster productivity and demonstrates proportionate response. It beats option C by being specific about feature-level suspension rather than a full shutdown, and it beats option B by escalating immediately rather than waiting for the fix to be confirmed — which is required because self-disclosure obligation timelines may not accommodate the delay.
